results.name: odd_vs_even_set_parity_violation
results.description: In parity-homogeneous sets of >=3 examples (excluding sets whose examples all end in 0 or 5), yes-rate for opposite-parity targets (>=10 away, no shared final digit) in all-odd sets minus that in all-even sets; observed > null means people treat 'odd' as a much weaker/less salient rule than 'even' (the model's parity attention is symmetric), observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: odd_vs_even_set_parity_violation
# description: In parity-homogeneous sets of >=3 examples (excluding sets whose examples all end in 0 or 5), yes-rate for opposite-parity targets (>=10 away, no shared final digit) in all-odd sets minus that in all-even sets; observed > null means people treat 'odd' as a much weaker/less salient rule than 'even' (the model's parity attention is symmetric), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    dist = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    dig = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    isex = (t == e).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    kin = (pres & (np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int)) >= 3)).any(1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    par = np.where(pres, np.mod(e1, 2), np.nan)
    pmax = np.nanmax(par, 1)
    pmin = np.nanmin(par, 1)
    round_set = ((np.mod(e1, 5) == 0) | ~pres).all(1)
    homog = (pmax == pmin) & (n >= 3) & ~round_set
    viol = (np.mod(t1, 2) != pmax) & (dist >= 10) & ~dig
    return rate(homog & (pmax == 1) & viol) - rate(homog & (pmax == 0) & viol)

results.name: mixed_set_round_target_contrast
results.description: In sets of >=2 examples where some but not all examples end in 0 or 5 (e.g. 15,11; 6,25), yes-rate for multiple-of-10 targets (>=10 away, no shared final digit) minus yes-rate for non-round unrelated targets (>=10 away, no shared digit, not multiple/divisor/gcd>=3 kin); observed < null means the model's round-number kinship route over-generalizes from a lone 5-ending example inside a mixed set, observed > null means it under-credits round targets there.
results.code:

    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    dist = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    dig = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    isex = (t == e).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    kin = (pres & (np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int)) >= 3)).any(1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    end5 = (np.mod(e1, 5) == 0) & pres
    mixed = (n >= 2) & end5.any(1) & ~(end5 | ~pres).all(1)
    base = mixed & (dist >= 10) & ~dig
    roundt = np.mod(t1, 10) == 0
    return rate(base & roundt) - rate(base & ~roundt & ~mult & ~divi & ~kin)

results.name: near_target_set_size_contrast
results.description: Yes-rate for near targets (1-9 from the nearest example, no shared final digit) in single-example sets minus in 3-4-example sets; observed > null means extra examples dilute near-target support more than the model's n^-kappa averaging predicts, observed < null means the model's averaging over-dilutes near support in larger sets.

    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    dist = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    dig = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    isex = (t == e).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    kin = (pres & (np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int)) >= 3)).any(1)

    near = (dist >= 1) & (dist <= 9) & ~dig
    return rate(near & (n == 1)) - rate(near & (n >= 3))

results.name: within_item_trial_drift
results.description: Correlation between trial_index and the rating after subtracting each (set, target) cell's mean rating; observed > null means people become more liberal (more yes) later in the session, observed < null more conservative/fatigued, a time trend the stationary model cannot produce.

results.name: large_example_multiple_contrast
results.description: Among targets >=10 from every example sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for multiples of some example >=13 (but of no example 2-12) minus yes-rate for unrelated targets (not multiple/divisor/gcd>=3 kin); observed < null means the model's size-independent multiples route over-credits multiples of two-digit examples (people use only times-table multiples), observed > null means it under-credits them.

# name: large_example_multiple_contrast
# description: Among targets >=10 from every example sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for multiples of some example >=13 (but of no example 2-12) minus yes-rate for unrelated targets (not multiple/divisor/gcd>=3 kin); observed < null means the model's size-independent multiples route over-credits multiples of two-digit examples (people use only times-table multiples), observed > null means it under-credits them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    dist = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    dig = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    isex = (t == e).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    kin = (pres & (np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int)) >= 3)).any(1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    small = (pres & (e1 >= 2) & (e1 <= 12) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    large = (pres & (e1 >= 13) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    base = (dist >= 10) & ~dig
    return rate(base & large & ~small) - rate(base & ~mult & ~divi & ~kin)

results.name: background_set_rate_sd

    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    dist = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    dig = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    isex = (t == e).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)

    kin = (pres & (np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int)) >= 3)).any(1)
    def rate(m):

    s = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].to_numpy()[bg], "r": r[bg]})
    g = s.groupby("s")["r"].agg(["mean", "count"])
    g = g[g["count"] >= 5]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

results.name: rule_consistent_distance_corr
results.description: In sets of >=3 examples with a shared rule (common final digit; else set gcd>=3; else common parity), correlation between distance to the nearest example and rating among non-example targets that obey the rule; observed > null (flatter/less negative) means people apply the rule all-or-none regardless of magnitude while the model keeps a similarity gradient, observed < null means the gradient is even steeper than the model's.
results.code:
# name: rule_consistent_distance_corr
# description: In sets of >=3 examples with a shared rule (common final digit; else set gcd>=3; else common parity), correlation between distance to the nearest example and rating among non-example targets that obey the rule; observed > null (flatter/less negative) means people apply the rule all-or-none regardless of magnitude while the model keeps a similarity gradient, observed < null means the gradient is even steeper than the model's.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    dist = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    dig = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    isex = (t == e).any(1)
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    kin = (pres & (np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int)) >= 3)).any(1)
    def rate(m):
        return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    ei = e1.astype(int)
    u = np.where(pres, np.mod(ei, 10), -1)
    umax = np.where(pres, u, -1).max(1)
    umin = np.where(pres, u, 99).min(1)
    same_digit = (umax == umin)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(np.where(pres, ei, 0), axis=1)
    par = np.where(pres, np.mod(ei, 2), -1)
    pmax = par.max(1)
    pmin = np.where(pres, par, 9).min(1)
    same_par = pmax == pmin
    ti = t1.astype(int)
    big = n >= 3
    obey = np.where(same_digit, np.mod(ti, 10) == umax,
           np.where(g >= 3, np.mod(ti, np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0,
           np.where(same_par, np.mod(ti, 2) == pmax, False)))
    m = big & obey & ~isex
    if m.sum() < 5 or np.std(r[m]) == 0 or np.std(dist[m]) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(dist[m], r[m])[0, 1])
